strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: benchmark compression when only a handful of source models are available, which is common for newly released benchmarks.

Extensive experimental validation across five benchmarks (text-only and multimodal) and 200+ models, with numerous ablations covering source pool size, source composition/diversity, coreset budget scaling (up to K=200), temporal distribution shift, and run-to-run stability (Appendix C).

The item-level Agreement metric (Appendix C.1) is a thoughtful addition that reveals a real weakness of MAE as a sole metric (GP-IRT can achieve low MAE via averaging/cancellation while missing per-item correctness patterns), strengthening the empirical case for the proposed method.

The spectral/interpretability analysis (Section 4) with a rigorous dual-granularity statistical protocol (Spearman + Kruskal-Wallis, difficulty-stratified analysis, FDR correction) provides reasonably convincing evidence that the aligned latent space encodes structure beyond simple difficulty, which is a genuine analytical contribution.
Model pools are fully listed (Appendix D), and implementation/protocol details (splits, decoding, formulas for discrimination/difficulty) are specified in enough detail to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: A core conceptual gap: the extrapolation stage (Section 2.4, Eq. 6-8), which produces the final accuracy predictions used for the headline ρ/MAE metrics, uses only a scalar feature x_i (average correctness across source models) — it does NOT use hidden states or aligned embeddings at all. The paper's central claim that hidden states provide a "dense signal" superior to discrete labels is therefore only exploited in the coreset-selection/clustering stage, not in extrapolation itself, which weakens the framing that richer internal representations directly drive the estimation gains.

Improvements over the strongest baseline (GP-IRT) are often modest and inconsistent in sign: e.g., Table 1 SEED-Bench K=10 shows GP-IRT beating REPCORE on ρ (0.594 vs 0.642 favors REPCORE but with high MAE difference is small), and Table 6 (larger budgets K=100-200) shows GP-IRT matching or slightly beating REPCORE on MAE. This tempers the significance of the claimed "consistent gains."

The discrete-representation ablation (Table 12/Appendix C.3) shows that replacing continuous embeddings with binary correctness vectors in the clustering stage yields only small performance differences in many cases, suggesting the practical value of the continuous hidden-state representation for the actual downstream task may be more limited than the motivating narrative implies.

No discussion or quantification of the computational/infrastructural overhead of extracting and storing hidden states (which requires model internals access, GPU memory, and per-item storage of high-dimensional vectors) compared to simply recording binary correctness labels — an important practical cost that is not weighed against the benchmark-compression cost savings the paper is motivated by.

The method is inherently restricted to open-weight/white-box models where hidden states are accessible; the conclusion acknowledges extension to closed-source models as future work, but this is a significant limitation on applicability that could be discussed more directly as a scope limitation rather than deferred entirely to future work.

Design choices such as using only the final layer's hidden state of the final output token are not ablated against alternative layer/token choices, leaving open whether the specific extraction choice is important or arbitrary.

The claim of evaluating "over 200 models" is somewhat inflated by counting overlapping model families across benchmarks rather than distinct architectures; this framing in the abstract could be clarified.

Main results tables (Table 1, 3, etc.) do not report variance/error bars in-line, deferring stability analysis entirely to appendix figures, which makes it harder to judge statistical significance of the reported margins from the main text alone.

The Impact Statement is boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with potential implications (e.g., risks of under-evaluating models on compressed benchmarks, or misuse of coresets to game leaderboard rankings).

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: benchmark compression under source-model scarcity, which is common for newly released benchmarks.

The core idea of using continuous hidden-state representations instead of sparse binary correctness vectors to recover item geometry is intuitive and reasonably novel relative to prior IRT/AnchorPoints-style approaches.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: 5 benchmarks (text and multimodal), 200+ models, multiple coreset budgets (K=10 to 200), and numerous ablations (source pool size, source composition/diversity, capability range, temporal drift, discrete vs. continuous clustering inputs).
The item-level Agreement metric is a thoughtful addition that exposes a real weakness of MAE as a sole metric (error cancellation in GP-IRT), improving the rigor of the evaluation.

Section 4's spectral/statistical analysis (global vs. difficulty-stratified association with subtask/ability labels) is a genuine attempt to interpret what the learned latent space captures beyond a trivial difficulty proxy, going beyond typical coreset papers that only report downstream numbers.
Good reproducibility support: detailed appendix with model lists per benchmark, hyperparameter/architecture specification, and formalized statistical aggregation procedures.
weaknesses: Improvements over baselines (especially GP-IRT) are often small in absolute terms (e.g., ρ gains of 0.01–0.03, overlapping MAE) and the advantage largely disappears or reverses at larger coreset budgets (Table 6, K≥100), raising questions about the practical significance of the method at budgets that are still quite cheap to evaluate.

The method fundamentally requires white-box access to model hidden states, which precludes its use for closed-source/API-only models — a major practical limitation compared to purely output-based baselines like AnchorPoints/GP-IRT; this is only mentioned as future work rather than discussed as a core limitation.

The extrapolation stage (Section 2.4) discards the learned aligned embeddings entirely and instead regresses from a single scalar average-correctness feature (Eq. 6); the representation-learning contribution is thus only used for coreset selection, not for the final extrapolation, which somewhat decouples the paper's central claim (hidden states carry richer signal) from the actual predictor used to produce final estimates.

No baseline comparison against other internal/feature-based methods discussed in the related work (e.g., EffiEval, SMART), despite these being directly relevant alternatives; only AnchorPoints, GP-IRT, and Random are compared.

Statistical significance claims in Section 4 rely on p/q-values that routinely underflow to numerical precision limits, which is more indicative of large sample size than of meaningfully large effect sizes; the interpretive claims (e.g., 'persistent structural signal') could be overstated without accompanying effect-size context normalized for scale.

The added computational/engineering overhead of extracting and storing hidden states across many models (vs. simple binary labels), and the cost of training model-specific projection layers + MLP per benchmark, is not analyzed or compared against baseline compute costs.
The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with potential considerations of this benchmarking infrastructure work.

strengths: Identifies and clearly motivates a practical gap in benchmark compression literature: existing coreset methods rely on output-only signals that become statistically unstable when only a handful of source models are available (e.g., for newly released benchmarks).

Extremely thorough empirical evaluation: 5 benchmarks (text and multimodal), 200+ models, multiple coreset budgets, and an unusually large set of ablations covering MLP architecture sensitivity, source pool size, source composition (family/capability diversity), scalability to larger budgets, temporal distribution shift, and partial hidden-state availability (masking).

The item-level Agreement metric (Appendix C.1) is a useful diagnostic that convincingly shows GP-IRT's competitive MAE can mask worse per-item fidelity, strengthening the case that ranking/agreement, not just MAE, matters.

The spectral/interpretability analysis (Section 4) with a well-specified statistical protocol (global vs. difficulty-stratified association, Stouffer aggregation, FDR correction) provides non-trivial evidence that the learned latent space encodes more than scalar difficulty (task type/ability mode persist after stratification), and this is validated functionally via the PC ablation for extrapolation.

Honest and constructive limitations section (Section 6): explicitly discusses the hidden-state access requirement (excluding closed/API-only models) and probes robustness via a well-designed masking experiment (random vs. adversarial-distance masking) rather than merely asserting the limitation.
Reproducibility support is reasonably strong: architecture/training details, data splits, wall-clock/storage overhead measurements, and full model-pool listings are provided.
weaknesses: The improvements over the strongest output-based baseline (GP-IRT) are often modest in absolute terms (e.g., MAE differences of 0.002–0.01 in several settings), and GP-IRT is frequently competitive or better on MAE, with the paper's rebuttal relying mainly on the Agreement metric; this makes the practical significance of the gains somewhat less compelling than the framing suggests.

The central motivating claim of robustness to extreme source scarcity is only partially supported by Table 3: performance is fairly flat from |S|=5 to |S|=20 for RepCore, but GP-IRT is already reasonably strong at |S|=10 (the main experimental setting), narrowing the practical case for the method except at very small |S| (e.g., 5).

The technical contribution is somewhat incremental — a per-model linear projection into a shared space followed by a shared MLP trained with cross-entropy supervision is a fairly standard representation-alignment/probing recipe (similar to prior probing work cited in Appendix A.2); the novelty lies mainly in the application to coreset selection rather than in new methodology.

The extrapolation stage (Section 2.4) does not actually use the learned hidden-state embeddings for unseen items — it relies on a scalar averaged source correctness feature (xi) and per-target ridge regression, so the paper's central selling point (rich continuous hidden-state signal) is exploited only for coreset selection, not for the final score extrapolation, which weakens the coherence of the overall pipeline's story.

Auxiliary but topically relevant baselines (EffiEval, TailoredBench) are excluded from the main comparison table and diagnostic ablations with a somewhat post-hoc justification (their assumptions are 'fragile' in this setting), which risks selectively favoring the primary baselines the method was tuned against.

The method fundamentally requires white-box access to hidden states of source models, which the paper acknowledges limits applicability to closed/API-only models; while the masking analysis is a reasonable probe, it does not resolve the core practical restriction for many real-world evaluation settings involving proprietary models.

Some of the statistical-significance claims in Section 4/Appendix B.2 (p-values near floating-point underflow across ~100 model snapshots aggregated over thousands of items) are somewhat inflated in apparent rigor, since with very large effective sample sizes even small/weak associations become 'significant'; effect sizes (already reported) are more informative than the extreme p-value magnitudes emphasized in the text.
